segments.text: A good GPU can cost more than a used car.
A dashboard could say it's 95% busy,
and the language model running on it can still be slow.
Most of that busy time is spent waiting.
Picture the fastest chef in the world,
working in a kitchen where every ingredient lives in a storeroom across town.
For every single bite, the chef walks there and back.
Chopping takes no time at all, and the walking takes the whole day.
That's what happens inside a language model for every word it writes,
and we'll keep coming back to this kitchen for the rest of the video.
We'll look at exactly what the chip is waiting for.
Once we know, most speed advice gets easier to judge,
and when someone shows us a new trick,
we can tell in about two minutes whether it can help.
Let's start with the weights of an LLM.
Once training ends, they're frozen,
and serving the model means doing math with them over and over for every request.
The whole video rests on one fact.
To write a single token,
the computer has to read almost all of those weights out of memory.
A token is a small piece of text,
a word or part of a word or even a space,
and in English it averages about four letters or three quarters of a word.
A dense model uses all of its weights on every token,
so there's no shortcut,
and every trip visits the entire storeroom.
Let's put numbers on it.
Each weight takes about two bytes,
so a model with n billion weights means two n gigabytes to read for every token.
Memory bandwidth is how fast the GPU can pull data out of its own memory,
like the width of the road to the storeroom,
and we'll call it b.
That gives us a speed limit.
The most tokens per second we can ever get is b divided by 2n.
Say a model has 10 billion weights, which is 20 gigabytes.
If memory moves 2000 gigabytes a second,
then 2000 divided by 20 is 100,
so we get 100 tokens per second at most.
No clever code beats that,
because the numbers physically have to travel.
Next, we compare the speed we actually measure to that limit,
because the gap tells us what to fix.
If we're close to it, we're memory bound,
which means the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data.
That's the chef on the road.
The only way to speed up is to carry less on each trip,
so we move fewer bytes.
Faster chopping would change nothing,
since the chef spends almost no time chopping.
If we're five or ten times below the limit,
the road isn't where the time goes.
Maybe the chef keeps stopping to look for the recipe,
or the kitchen is cooking one tiny dish at a time.
On a GPU, that shows up as overhead, idle time,
and work too small to fill the chip,
and carrying less won't touch any of it.
It's easy to spend weeks compressing a model
while sitting 10 times below the limit,
where saving bytes never mattered.
A 30-second calculation before we optimize anything prevents that.
To see why a GPU can look busy and still be mostly idle,
start with how it's built.
A GPU is made for huge, parallel jobs,
like a kitchen with 2000 burners,
and decoding for a single user puts one pot on one of them.
The kitchen is running, and almost all of it is idle.
Three things that confuse people follow from this.
First, the utilization meter misleads us.
95% busy means only that some job is on the chip,
and says nothing about how much of the chip is working.
A GPU can be 95% busy and 2% full.
Second, serving many users at once is the main lever we have,
and it's called batching.
We read the weights once and use them for 50 users,
so a single trip to the storeroom feeds 50 orders.
Third, speeding up a single user is very hard.
There's nothing to batch, so the memory limit applies in full.
Every request also has two jobs that look alike and behave very differently.
Prefill reads the prompt.
The model handles all of it at once,
so a 5000-token prompt is processed together,
and the GPU loves this.
The chip is truly full,
and the math is the limit,
which is what compute bound means.
Decode writes the answer, one token at a time,
because each token depends on the one before.
This is the one-pot job from the kitchen,
and it's memory bound.
Whenever someone shows us an optimization,
we ask whether it helps prefill or decode.
If they can't say, they probably don't fully understand it.
These two jobs give us three numbers to track,
and a restaurant makes them easy to see.
Time to first token is how long until the first dish arrives,
and it depends on prefill and on waiting in line.
Time per output token is how fast the rest of the meal comes
once it starts, and it depends on decode.
Throughput is total tokens per second across all users,
the customers served per hour.
We can't max out all three.
Packing more users into a batch raises throughput
and makes everyone wait longer for that first dish.
So we pick a priority before touching any settings.
A chat app needs to feel fast,
a batch job cares only about cost,
and an agent makes a long chain of calls,
so any slowness repeats at every step.
We write the choice down,
because weeks into tuning it's easy to forget.
Sometimes a model is too big for one GPU,
or one GPU's memory bandwidth isn't enough,
and we split it across several.
There are four ways.
Tensor parallelism slices every layer into pieces,
one piece per GPU.
A layer is one stage of the model,
like one floor of a tall building.
Each GPU now reads only part of the weights,
so four GPUs means four roads working together
and a higher speed limit.
The cost is that after each step,
the GPUs have to share their results,
at least twice per layer for every token.
Inside one machine,
a fast link called NVLink makes this quick,
but between machines the link is much slower
and usually eats the whole gain,
so we keep tensor parallelism inside one machine.
Pipeline parallelism splits by layers instead,
like an assembly line.
The first GPU holds the first group of layers,
the next holds the next group,
and only a small hand-off passes between them,
so slower connections work fine.
The catch is bubbles,
moments when a station sits idle
waiting on the one before it.
Heavy traffic hides most of them,
while a single request feels every one.
We use this when we have to cross machines.
Data parallelism makes full copies of the model
and shares the requests between them.
No single user gets faster,
but we serve more people.
There's a trap though.
If turn one of a chat goes to copy A
and turn two goes to copy B,
copy B has never seen the conversation
and starts from zero.
Dashboards look healthy while real throughput drops,
so we send each conversation back to the same copy.
Expert parallelism is for mixture of experts models,
which have many small subnetworks
and run only a few of them for each token.
Putting different experts on different GPUs
means each GPU reads far fewer bytes.
The costs are more traffic between GPUs
and uneven work,
since some experts get far more visitors than others.
To choose, we start simple.
If the model fits on one GPU with room to spare,
we use one GPU and add copies,
which is the easiest setup to run
and usually the best value.
If it doesn't fit,
we use tensor parallelism up to one machine,
and if it's still too big,
we add pipeline parallelism across machines.
For mixture of experts, we use expert parallelism.
Then we check one more number.
How much memory is left on each GPU
after the weights load?
That left over is the KV cache budget.
The KV cache is the model's working memory.
It's notes on everything it has read in this conversation,
and more room means more users at once
and longer conversations.
Two setups can look the same on a slide
and differ by two times here,
so we do the math.
Twice the GPUs never gives twice the speed.
Each new one adds more communication
and leaves every GPU with less to do,
so we measure what each one adds
and stop when the next isn't worth its price.
Next come four rules for how to approach all of this work.
Rule one is to profile before we theorize.
A profiler is a stopwatch for every part of a program.
The common mistake is believing a story that sounds right,
like the model is big so memory is the problem,
or the GPUs talk a lot so speed up the talking.
Both are wrong more often than we'd expect.
Time spent also isn't the same as time that matters.
If we boil pasta while we chop onions,
boiling the water faster doesn't get dinner ready sooner.
Because the chopping is what we're waiting on.
Overlapping work costs nothing,
and one clue is a profile whose percentages add up to more than 100.
If we profile on day one,
20 minutes can rule out whole piles of ideas.
Rule two is to find the equation,
then work on the equation.
We can't push on speed directly,
so we break it into two or three pieces we can measure,
like work finished per cycle divided by time per cycle.
We change one setting and watch both pieces.
Then we test ourselves.
If we built the fit from settings four and eight,
we predict six and then try six.
If it holds, we understand the system.
We also work out each idea's ceiling before testing it.
If the best case is a 10% win and we need 40, we skip it.
Most ideas fail this check in five minutes for free.
Rule three is to be suspicious of trade-offs.
A bigger batch raises throughput and raises waiting time.
Lower precision, which means storing numbers with fewer digits,
runs faster, but we have to ask whether the answer is still right.
We measure both sides.
If a change raises throughput by 30% and makes every step 80% slower, we lost.
Rule four is to keep a log, especially of what did nothing.
A realistic ratio is a couple of ideas that work for every dozen that don't,
and each dead end removes a branch from the search only if we write down why it failed.
With those rules in place, here's the order to build things in.
The payoff drops fast as we go down this list,
and the interesting items at the bottom are tempting, so we work from the top.
Step one is to use a real inference server.
That's software built for running models for many users,
and VLLM and SG-Lang are the two big ones.
If we're serving with a handmade loop, we switch.
And that change alone can give several times the speed.
The main gain is continuous batching.
The old way waits for a whole group to finish before starting the next,
like a restaurant that won't seat anyone new until every table is paid.
Continuous batching swaps a finished request out and a waiting one in at every step,
and it's usually the largest single gain in model serving.
The server provides it for free.
Step two is to cache the prefixes.
Chats repeat themselves, so turn ten sends the first nine turns again.
A prefix is the beginning of a prompt,
and the server keeps that already processed beginning in the KV cache,
so it doesn't redo the work.
Finding it already stored is called a cache hit.
There are two mistakes to avoid.
Caches match from the start, so the part that stays the same goes first,
and the part that changes goes last.
And a timestamp at the top of a system prompt makes every request a miss.
The second is treating hit rate as a gentle dial.
Going from 98% to 97% sounds tiny,
but the uncached part is what the GPU actually works on,
so that one point can mean tens of percent more real work.
We watch the amount of uncached work, not just the percentage.
Step three is to reduce the bytes.
We know decode is memory bound, so fewer bytes means more speed.
Quantization stores numbers with fewer digits, like rounding 3.14159 to 3.14.
Applied to the weights, it makes the model smaller,
and applied to the KV cache, it fits more users on the same machine.
Software can claim to support a format and still quietly take a slow path, so we check the speed.
Quantization also changes what the model computes, so we owe an accuracy check.
Step four is speculative decoding.
Decode is slow because it writes one token at a time,
but checking is fast because the GPU can check many tokens at once.
A small, quick model, the prep cook, drafts the next few tokens,
and the big model, the head chef, checks all of them in one pass.
Right guesses stay, and at the first wrong one, we throw out the rest.
To know whether it helps, we use one formula.
Speed equals tokens accepted per pass divided by time per pass.
Three things follow from that.
There's a ceiling, since if we guess K tokens ahead,
we can never get more than K plus one tokens in a pass.
Guessing further has a cost, because every extra guess adds time
and is less likely to be right, so the sweet spot is usually small.
And the small model has to think like the big one,
or its guesses get rejected and we paid for nothing.
Checking also gets more expensive when the prompt is long,
to the point where it can cost more than it earns.
If a setup offers a relaxed mode that keeps guesses the strict check would reject,
we treat it as a different product, with its own column in the results.
Step five is kernels and graphs.
To write one token, the GPU doesn't do one big job.
It does hundreds of small ones in a row.
Multiply these numbers, add those, rescale the result.
Each of those small jobs is called a kernel.
The GPU doesn't decide what to do next on its own,
because the computer's main processor, the CPU, has to tell it.
That's a manager, calling out orders to the chef,
chop the onions, stir the pot, add salt.
Some of these jobs are tiny.
The chef finishes add salt in a blink,
but the manager still has to say it out loud, which takes just as long.
So the chef spends a lot of time standing around waiting for the next order.
The fix is to hand over the whole recipe card once,
and let the chef run it again and again, one token after another.
Recording the card once and replaying it is called Graph Capture.
Most servers have it, so we make sure it's on.
There are two warnings here.
Some settings fix a crash by turning off an optimization everywhere,
and we can lose several times the speed,
so we look for a setting that turns off only the broken piece.
Compilers, which rewrite code to run faster,
often by merging small steps together, need the same care.
We profile first, and if the work they could merge is 2% of the total time,
the best possible win is 2%.
We should also expect some trouble with software versions.
Libraries can each work fine alone and still clash with each other,
so we pin versions, locking each one to a specific release, so nothing changes on us.
Benchmarking comes next,
and whatever number a benchmark gives us is probably wrong in one of a few ways.
First, a benchmark measures the workload we give it, not just the server.
Unique requests force the server to start from scratch,
requests with a shared prefix let the cache absorb most of the work,
and random prompt tests model traffic nobody has.
If we can, we replay real sessions, in order,
so the cache behaves like production, and we use plenty of them.
With only 50 recorded chats, a big test cycles through the same ones,
and the hit rate looks great for the wrong reason.
Second, the load we aim for isn't the load we get.
If we aim for 2000 requests a minute and measure 1100,
the cause is often the load generator,
the program that plays fake users falling behind.
We report both numbers.
Third, a headline number needs a breakdown.
The huge tokens per minute figure might be 97% input,
mostly cache hits, which are data read back rather than computed.
That's fair for can we absorb this traffic,
and misleading for how much compute did we do.
So we say which one we mean.
Fourth, percentiles are noisy.
P99 says 99 out of 100 requests were faster than that number,
and it bounces around, especially on small samples.
We report it because users feel it,
but we base conclusions on steadier numbers,
like work per cycle and cache hit rate.
We also control the environment.
One workload, one setup, one change at a time.
We warm up first, and we repeat runs and report the spread,
because the best of 10 tells us little.
We read the settings back from the running server,
since a folder called fastconfig version 3 final will eventually lie.
One more thing is easy to skip.
Most serious optimisations change what the model computes,
so every speed claim needs an accuracy claim.
We run the same tests on two servers that differ only in the optimisation,
on the same day, because last quarter's published scores aren't a baseline.
We use several tests covering different skills, since damage is uneven.
A model can keep its general knowledge and still break structured output,
which means answers in a strict format that a program can read.
We repeat the tests to get error bars,
which show the range where the true score probably sits.
If that range comfortably includes zero difference,
the honest report is no measurable difference,
and that says more than a bear, no regression.
We also test the shape of the answer,
because things break in structure.
Fields land in the wrong place,
thinking text leaks into the answer,
and tool calls come out broken.
Three problems hide from generic tests.
The first is repetition that ends normally.
A model might repeat the same paragraph eight times,
then give the right answer and stop.
Nothing flags it, and it costs many times the tokens.
The second is behaviour over many turns.
The safeguards on each request start fresh every turn,
so they can't see a mistake from three turns ago,
and we have to test whole conversations.
The third is failures that come and go.
If we run the test 20 times, we can say it fails 15% of the time.
It failed once is only a story.
Finally, the test suite has to be easy to run.
One file, no strange dependencies,
and a clear fail signal,
so a failed test stops the script
instead of hiding in the output.
If it's hard to run,
nobody will run it on the night it matters.
If we only remember five things,
they should be these.
One, work out the memory speed limit
before optimising anything,
because being near it and being far from it
are different problems.
Two, profile on day one.
Time spent isn't time that matters,
and overlapped work is free.
Three, batch and cache first.
They're the least exciting items on the list,
and they usually give more
than everything below them combined.
Four, find the equation behind the metric we care about.
Check it on a point we held out,
and work out each idea's ceiling before testing it.
Five, back every speed claim with an accuracy claim.
Measured against a baseline,
we ran ourselves,
on the same day, with error bars.
A couple of ideas will work,
and a dozen will do nothing,
and the notes on why each one failed
will outlast whatever setup we end up with.
Let's go measure the speed limit,
and see where we land.
